title: Inherited Thrombophilia: What Tips the Balance and When to Test
summary: How antithrombin, protein C and protein S deficiencies and the factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A variants tip the clotting balance, why functional tests mislead during a clot, on anticoagulants or in pregnancy, and which defects need DNA testing.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 38 Hits 3–11 and 14 and Traps 1, 2, 3 and 5. Checked against Nakashima & Rogers 2014, Khider 2022, Middeldorp 2023 (ASH guideline), Reardon 2026, Ozturk Ari 2026, Khan & Dickerman 2006 and Kakagia 2014. The reviewer’s fold-risks for homozygous FVL (10–15×) and FVL + OCPs (8–20×) differ from other sources (register flag rv-fvl-risk), so the lesson teaches the multiplying principle without one number. Not taught: “free protein S falls from the 10th week to ~60%” (sources say lower in the 2nd–3rd trimester, no figure), “+15–30% prothrombin” (sources give ~30%), the claim that factor II activity assays are blind to G20210A, and the ACMG/ACOG attribution for MTHFR (not read).

objectives: Describe how antithrombin, protein C and protein S restrain coagulation, including the free/bound split of protein S.
Explain how loss-of-function deficiencies and the FVL and G20210A variants tip the balance, and why risks combine.
Choose the right time for functional thrombophilia tests and recognize acute-phase, drug and pregnancy effects.
Choose activity vs antigen vs DNA testing for each defect, including type II deficiencies.

A request slip: “Full thrombophilia panel — today.” Result tokens drop in: protein C activity 45% (low); free protein S 38% (low); antithrombin 62% (low); factor VIII 210% (high). A question token: “Which of these results can you trust?” The cartoon scientist raises an eyebrow.

cues.text: A 34-year-old woman had a deep vein thrombosis four days ago. She is on heparin, and warfarin has just started.
The team orders a full thrombophilia panel today. Protein C is low, free protein S is low, antithrombin is low, and factor VIII is high.
Four abnormal results. Does she have four inherited clotting disorders? Or can you trust none of them yet?

props.label: Which of these results can you trust?

scenes.title: The brakes on clotting
scenes.altText: A balance (schematic): on one pan, procoagulant factors (thrombin, Va, VIIIa); on the other, three brakes. Antithrombin card: a serpin that inactivates thrombin and Xa; heparin greatly speeds it; not vitamin K dependent. Protein C card: vitamin K dependent; activated protein C (APC) cuts factors Va and VIIIa. Protein S card: APC’s cofactor, also vitamin K dependent; a pie splits ~40% free / ~60% bound to C4b-binding protein — only free protein S is functionally available. The pans stay level.

cues.text: Clotting is a balance. Thrombin and the activated cofactors V and VIII push toward a clot. Three natural brakes push back.
Antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa. Heparin speeds it up enormously. It is made in the liver but is not vitamin K dependent.
Protein C is vitamin K dependent. Once activated, activated protein C cuts factors Va and VIIIa, shutting down thrombin production.
Protein S is its cofactor, also vitamin K dependent. About 40 percent circulates free; about 60 percent is bound to C4b-binding protein.
Only the free fraction is functionally available, which is why labs usually measure free protein S. With all three brakes working, the pans stay level.

scenes.title: How the balance tips
scenes.altText: The balance tilts. Loss-of-function bin: antithrombin, protein C or protein S deficiency, autosomal dominant; antithrombin heterozygotes (functional levels ~35–70%) still clot — the highest VTE risk among the hereditary thrombophilias. Gain-of-function bin: factor V Leiden — factor Va resists cleavage by APC (heterozygote risk roughly 5-fold); prothrombin G20210A (F2 c.*97G>A) — about 30% more prothrombin made (heterozygote ~3-fold). A stack of weights: inherited defect + estrogen or pregnancy — risks combine, and published fold-increases vary widely. A warfarin clock: protein C falls before the longer-lived procoagulant factors → microthrombi in skin venules (warfarin-induced skin necrosis), linked to protein C deficiency.

cues.text: Loss of a brake tips the balance. Antithrombin, protein C and protein S deficiencies are inherited as autosomal dominant traits.
Even one bad copy matters. Antithrombin heterozygotes run at roughly 35 to 70 percent and still clot. It carries the highest risk of the hereditary thrombophilias.

Or the accelerator sticks. In factor V Leiden, activated protein C cannot cut factor Va efficiently, about a fivefold risk in heterozygotes. Prothrombin G20210A makes about 30 percent more prothrombin, about threefold.
Risks stack. Factor V Leiden plus estrogen or pregnancy raises the risk far more than either alone. Published multipliers vary widely by study, so learn the principle, not one number.

Warfarin has a trap of its own. Protein C falls faster than the longer-lived clotting factors, so for a few days the balance tips toward clotting. In protein C deficiency that can cause warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

lines: AT · protein C · protein S deficiency

scenes.title: When to test, and with which assay
scenes.altText: A timeline: “clot / on anticoagulant” zone marked ✗ for functional tests — acute thrombosis consumes regulators, acute phase raises factor VIII and fibrinogen, unfractionated heparin can lower antithrombin activity up to ~30%, warfarin lowers protein C and S, DOACs interfere with clot-based assays, pregnancy and estrogen lower protein S. A ✓ zone: at least 4–6 weeks after the event and off therapy; abnormal results repeated on a new specimen. A DNA token sits above both zones: genotyping is unaffected. Method cards: APC-resistance ratio → confirm factor V Leiden by DNA; prothrombin G20210A → PCR genotyping; protein C, protein S and antithrombin → activity (functional) assay first — an antigen-only assay misses type II (normal antigen, low activity). Back to the patient: today, only DNA tests are interpretable.

cues.text: Timing is the first test. A fresh clot uses up regulators, and the acute phase pushes factor VIII and fibrinogen up.
Drugs distort too. Unfractionated heparin can lower antithrombin activity, warfarin lowers proteins C and S, and DOACs interfere with clot-based assays. Pregnancy and estrogen lower protein S.
So functional tests wait: at least four to six weeks after the event and off anticoagulants, and any abnormal result is repeated on a new specimen. DNA tests are not affected.
Method matters. A low APC-resistance ratio is confirmed by factor V Leiden DNA testing. Prothrombin G20210A is found only by genotyping.

For proteins C, S and antithrombin, start with an activity assay. An antigen-only test misses type II, where the protein is present but does not work. For our patient today, only the DNA tests can be read.

props.label: DNA genotyping: valid in either zone

scenes.title: Four classic traps
scenes.altText: Four trap cards appear in turn: “Low protein C on day 4 of warfarin = protein C deficiency” (✓ retest off therapy; DNA tests are the exception); “Low free protein S at 28 weeks’ pregnancy = deficiency” (✓ protein S is physiologically lower in pregnancy — retest afterward); “Screen for G20210A with a factor II level” (✓ genotype by PCR); “Add MTHFR to the panel” (✓ ASH 2023: MTHFR polymorphisms have been shown not to be associated with VTE).

cues.text: Trap one: low protein C during a clot or on warfarin means deficiency. No. Retest when quiet and off therapy. Only DNA results stand.
Trap two: low free protein S in a pregnant patient means deficiency. Protein S is physiologically lower in pregnancy. Retest afterward.
Trap three: screen for prothrombin G20210A with a factor II level. The diagnostic test is DNA genotyping.
Trap four: add MTHFR to the panel. The 2023 ASH guideline says MTHFR variants have been shown not to be associated with venous thrombosis.

scenes.title: Proteins need peace; DNA doesn’t care
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Proteins need peace; DNA doesn’t care.” A protein token (PC, PS, AT, FVIII) sits under a storm cloud labelled clot · drugs · pregnancy; a DNA token (FVL, G20210A) sits unbothered. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: proteins need peace; DNA doesn’t care. Protein levels shift with clots, drugs and pregnancy; a genotype does not.

Where it breaks: a positive genotype is still not a reason to test everyone; lupus anticoagulant has its own timing rules; and guidelines favour selective testing only when the result would change management.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Functional tests (PC, PS, AT, FVIII): ≥ 4–6 weeks after the clot, off anticoagulants, not in pregnancy · activity assay first (type II)”, “FVL and G20210A: DNA, any time · MTHFR not associated with VTE”.

cues.text: Test proteins C, S and antithrombin with activity assays when the patient is quiet and off anticoagulants; find factor V Leiden and G20210A by DNA, any time.

props.label: PC · PS · AT: activity assay, ≥ 4–6 wk after clot, off anticoagulants, not pregnant
FVL (after low APC-R) · G20210A: DNA, any time · MTHFR: not a VTE marker

explanation.what: Plain language: thrombophilia is an inherited or acquired tendency to clot, caused by weak natural brakes or an overactive accelerator. Scientific terms: antithrombin (AT), protein C, activated protein C (APC), protein S, C4b-binding protein (C4BP), factor V Leiden (FVL, APC resistance), prothrombin G20210A (F2 c.*97G>A), type I (quantitative) vs type II (qualitative) deficiency.
explanation.why: AT inactivates thrombin and Xa (accelerated by heparin). APC, with free protein S as cofactor, cleaves Va and VIIIa. Deficiencies of AT, PC and PS are autosomal dominant; AT deficiency carries the highest hereditary VTE risk. FVL Va resists APC; G20210A raises prothrombin about 30%. Warfarin lowers protein C faster than the longer-lived procoagulant factors, causing a transient prothrombotic state and skin necrosis in protein C deficiency.
explanation.measure: Functional assays are distorted by acute thrombosis, the acute phase (↑FVIII, ↑fibrinogen), anticoagulants (UFH lowers AT activity up to ~30%; warfarin lowers PC, PS; DOACs interfere) and pregnancy/estrogen (↓PS). Test ≥ 4–6 weeks after the event or after stopping therapy; repeat abnormal results on a new specimen. DNA tests are unaffected. APC-R ratio: normal ≥ 2.0, heterozygote 1.5–2.0, homozygote < 1.5 (lab-specific cut-offs); confirm FVL by DNA. G20210A: PCR genotyping. PC, PS, AT: activity assays first; antigen-only misses type II.
explanation.differs: Type I deficiency: activity and antigen both low. Type II: antigen normal, activity low. Inherited vs acquired low PS: pregnancy, estrogen, inflammation and high FVIII lower PS. MTHFR polymorphisms: shown not to be associated with VTE (ASH 2023); hyperhomocysteinemia is measured separately.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: testing timing, low free PS in pregnancy, which defects need DNA, type II detection, warfarin skin necrosis, AT heterozygotes clotting, and MTHFR not belonging in a VTE panel.

comparisons.title: Type I vs type II protein C deficiency
comparisons.distinguisher: An activity assay detects both; an antigen-only assay misses type II.

comparisons.title: Functional tests vs DNA tests
comparisons.distinguisher: Timing rules apply to protein-level tests, not genotypes.

mnemonic.text: Proteins need peace; DNA doesn’t care.
mnemonic.explanation: Protein-level tests (PC, PS, AT, FVIII) shift with clots, anticoagulants and pregnancy, so test when quiet; genotypes (FVL, G20210A) do not change.
mnemonic.limitation: A genotype still needs a clinical reason to test; lupus anticoagulant has its own timing rules; guidelines favour selective testing only when the result changes management.

questions.stem: Four days after a DVT, a patient on heparin with warfarin just started has protein C 45%, free protein S 38% and antithrombin 62%. What is the best laboratory recommendation?

options.text: Repeat the functional tests on a new specimen at least 4–6 weeks after the event and off anticoagulants; DNA tests can be done now
options.rationale: Correct. Acute thrombosis, heparin and warfarin all lower these values; genotyping is unaffected.

options.text: Report combined protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low values during an acute clot and anticoagulation are expected and not diagnostic.

options.text: Report antithrombin deficiency only, since warfarin does not affect antithrombin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Warfarin does not lower AT, but unfractionated heparin and acute thrombosis can.

options.text: Switch to antigen assays, which are not affected by anticoagulants
options.rationale: Incorrect. Warfarin lowers protein C and S levels themselves, and antigen-only testing misses type II defects.

questions.stem: A woman at 28 weeks’ gestation, no history of thrombosis, has free protein S antigen 35%. Protein C and antithrombin are normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Likely physiologic lowering in pregnancy; retest after pregnancy if clinically needed
options.rationale: Correct. Protein S is lower in the second and third trimester; ASH 2023 advises testing before conception to avoid spurious protein S results.

options.text: Hereditary protein S deficiency, type I
options.rationale: Incorrect. Type I needs low total protein S antigen, confirmed outside pregnancy.

options.text: Factor V Leiden; order an APC-resistance assay
options.rationale: Incorrect. FVL does not lower protein S; pregnancy also affects clot-based APC-R assays.

options.text: Lab error; free protein S does not change in pregnancy

questions.stem: Off anticoagulants, with normal liver function and vitamin K status, a patient has low protein C activity and normal protein C antigen. Which conclusion fits?

options.rationale: Correct. The protein is present but does not work: normal antigen, low activity.
Incorrect. Type I has both antigen and activity reduced.

options.text: Normal; antigen is the definitive test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Antigen-only testing misses type II; activity assays are the screen.
Incorrect. G20210A raises prothrombin and is found by genotyping; it does not lower protein C.

claims.text: AT inactivates thrombin and Xa, accelerated by heparin, not vitamin K dependent; APC with free PS cleaves Va and VIIIa; ~40% PS free / ~60% C4BP-bound; free PS is the functional form.
AT, PC, PS deficiencies autosomal dominant; AT heterozygotes ~35–70% and highest hereditary risk; FVL ~5× heterozygous; G20210A ~30% more prothrombin, ~3×; risks rise with added factors.
Protein C falls faster than procoagulant factors after warfarin starts; skin necrosis associated with protein C deficiency.
Acute clot, acute phase, UFH, warfarin, DOACs and pregnancy distort functional tests; test ≥ 4–6 weeks after event/therapy and repeat abnormal results; DNA unaffected.
APC-R → FVL DNA confirmation; G20210A by PCR genotyping; activity assays first for PC/PS/AT; antigen-only misses type II.
MTHFR polymorphisms shown not to be associated with VTE.
Homozygous FVL 10–15×; FVL + OCP 8–20×, + pregnancy 25–40×; free PS falls from the 10th week to ~60%; factor II activity assays cannot detect G20210A; ACMG and ACOG recommend against MTHFR testing.
